Enforce authentication and role-based access control (including CRUD-level permissions) on MCP components and bind each session to an identity, since MCP leaves identity and RBAC optional and many implementations omit them.

Require codified approval workflows and force re-consent whenever a trusted MCP server's capabilities or data access change, so a previously benign, approved service cannot silently gain access to sensitive resources.
Enforce least privilege for every MCP server by using narrow scopes, per-server credentials, and short-lived secrets where the platform supports them.
Authenticate remote MCP endpoints and bind every session or token check to the current requester before authorizing tool execution.

Avoid making user-facing MCP authorization depend on local server setup and plaintext API credentials; use an authorization flow that removes manual credential provisioning from the normal path.
Treat LLM-based MCP clients as public OAuth clients and do not rely on a shipped client secret for client authentication.

Use OAuth rather than shared credentials or API keys when MCP agents need to access protected user resources, especially across remote or third-party boundaries.

Do not rely on any platform- or system-level authorization for MCP; unlike a centralized OS permission framework, MCP has no system-level authorization infrastructure, so each server must define and enforce its own authorization logic.

Assume any remote, potentially untrusted agent that can reach the MCP endpoint and speak the protocol can issue tool invocations (for example via mcp-remote to an HTTP endpoint); network reachability plus held authorization state is exploitable, even without controlling the server process or stealing credentials.

Apply dynamic validation only to the ambiguous case — tools whose execution paths already contain authorization logic — and unify deployment modes (SSE, stdio) non-invasively with an mcp-remote protocol proxy that captures inputs and outputs.

Select MCP transport by deployment target: stdio for local servers (low-latency, no network overhead) and HTTP/S with streaming for remote servers (adds standard authentication); do not assume one transport fits both.

Assess each MCP client's transport security via a connection fingerprint (supported modes, handshake, auth, session persistence): unencrypted persistent SSE can leak request headers, stdio can leak tokens through unsanitized logging, and hybrid-mode clients warrant extra scrutiny for unexpected data flows.
Expect stdio support in nearly all MCP clients (339 of 341) as the legacy default for local, synchronous communication inherited from early prototypes.

Build on OAuth 2.1 and the referenced RFC subset (RFC 8414, RFC 7591, RFC 9728, Client ID Metadata Documents) rather than inventing bespoke authorization; authorization servers MUST implement OAuth 2.1 with appropriate measures for both confidential and public clients.

Model the MCP server as an OAuth 2.1 resource server and the MCP client as an OAuth 2.1 client acting for a resource owner, and treat the authorization server as a separable component (co-hosted or standalone) located via metadata.

Require MCP servers to expose OAuth 2.0 Protected Resource Metadata (RFC 9728) containing at least one authorization_servers entry, and require clients to use Protected Resource Metadata for authorization-server discovery.

Require each authorization server to expose at least one of OAuth 2.0 Authorization Server Metadata (RFC 8414) or OpenID Connect Discovery 1.0, and require clients to support both discovery mechanisms.

Authorization servers should fetch and cache (respecting HTTP cache headers) URL-formatted client_ids and advertise client_id_metadata_document_supported; clients should check that capability, may authenticate with private_key_jwt, and may fall back to Dynamic Client Registration or pre-registration when CIMD is unavailable.
Follow OAuth 2.1 Section 7 security best practices end to end: implement secure token storage, issue short-lived access tokens, and rotate refresh tokens for public clients.
Drive MCP OAuth setup from standards-based discovery documents instead of hardcoded provider assumptions or service-specific configuration.
For OAuth-enabled MCP authorization, implement OAuth 2.1 with security controls suitable for both confidential and public clients.

Adopt the mid-2025 spec controls (OAuth2 Resource Server patterns and Resource Indicators, RFC 8707) to prevent token replay and ensure scope isolation, while not assuming peer servers comply given uneven adoption and backward-compatibility gaps.

Deliver Protected Resource Metadata via a WWW-Authenticate resource_metadata parameter on 401 responses or a well-known URI; clients MUST parse WWW-Authenticate headers, react to 401s, prefer the resource_metadata URL when present, and otherwise fall back to the well-known URIs in the specified order.

When using Client ID Metadata Documents, host the metadata at an HTTPS URL that contains a path and whose client_id equals the URL exactly, include at least client_id/client_name/redirect_uris, and have the authorization server validate the client_id-URL match, the presented redirect URIs, and that the document is well-formed JSON with the required fields.
Use a WWW-Authenticate metadata link for protected-resource discovery when a fixed well-known metadata endpoint is not appropriate, accepting the extra request this adds.
When an unauthenticated client reaches a protected MCP resource, return a 401 response that directs the client to the protected-resource metadata through WWW-Authenticate.

Advertise required scopes in the WWW-Authenticate scope parameter; clients MUST treat the challenge scopes as authoritative for the current request, MUST NOT assume any subset/superset relationship to scopes_supported, and MUST apply the scope-selection fallback when no scope is provided.

Follow least privilege in scope selection: request only necessary scopes, preferring the scope from the WWW-Authenticate challenge and otherwise requesting all scopes_supported (the intended minimal baseline), acquiring additional scopes incrementally via step-up authorization.

On a runtime insufficient-scope error, respond with 403 plus a Bearer WWW-Authenticate header carrying error=insufficient_scope, the required scope set, and resource_metadata; clients should react with a step-up authorization flow (user-delegated clients SHOULD, client_credentials clients MAY) using retry limits and tracked upgrade attempts, while servers keep a consistent, user-experience-aware scope-inclusion strategy.

Adopt a progressive least-privilege scope model: grant a minimal initial scope of low-risk read/discovery operations, elevate incrementally via targeted WWW-Authenticate scope challenges, tolerate down-scoped tokens, emit precise (not full-catalog) challenges with logged elevation events, and have clients start from baseline scopes while caching denied-scope failures.

Avoid scope anti-patterns and always enforce authorization server-side: do not publish every scope in scopes_supported, use wildcard/omnibus scopes, bundle unrelated privileges, or change scope semantics silently, and never treat scopes claimed in a token as sufficient without independent server-side authorization checks.

When discovering authorization-server metadata, clients MUST probe multiple well-known endpoints in the defined priority order, which differs depending on whether the issuer URL includes a path component.

Support the three client-registration mechanisms and, when several are available, select in priority order: pre-registered credentials, then Client ID Metadata Documents (if the AS advertises support), then Dynamic Client Registration (kept mainly for backwards compatibility), then prompt the user.
Consider URL-based client identifiers with client metadata documents when MCP needs client identity without a dynamic registration step.
Treat Dynamic Client Registration as a risky default for broad MCP interoperability unless the server and client lifecycle controls are explicit.
Use Dynamic Client Registration to onboard LLM clients without manual administrator pre-registration when MCP clients and services are numerous or frequently changing.

Support Dynamic Client Registration when an MCP client may connect to unfamiliar servers, especially in broad workbench-style environments.

Transmit access tokens only in the Authorization request header, never in the URI query string, and include authorization on every HTTP request from client to server even within one logical session.

MCP servers MUST validate every access token per OAuth 2.1 Section 5.2, accept only tokens whose intended audience is the server itself, return HTTP 401 for invalid or expired tokens, and never accept or transit tokens issued for other resources; clients MUST NOT send a server any token not issued by that server's authorization server.

Never pass tokens through: an MCP server must reject any access token that was not explicitly issued to itself, because token passthrough bypasses audience-bound security controls, breaks the audit trail, and enables use of the server as an exfiltration proxy.
Preserve MCP client bootstrap from a single server URL by using protected-resource metadata to point clients from the MCP resource server to the appropriate authorization server metadata.
Issue MCP access tokens for a specific MCP resource server audience and do not make the same token valid for both MCP and the service regular API.

Use a dedicated MCP authorization server as a delegation boundary when relying on external identity or OAuth services, so the MCP client sees MCP-specific endpoints while backend identity flows can vary.
Push login, token issuance, and related authorization complexity into the MCP authorization server so the MCP resource server can stay focused on validating tokens and serving protected resources.
Let the resource authorization server issue and validate its normal access tokens for the MCP server instead of requiring a universal Cross-App Access token format.
Publish protected-resource metadata for MCP resources with the resource identifier, trusted authorization servers, accepted bearer-token handling, and token verification material.
Validate Resource Indicators or equivalent audience binding on incoming tokens and reject tokens not issued for the MCP server.
Never forward the MCP client access token to upstream APIs; have the MCP server obtain service-appropriate upstream tokens as its own OAuth client.

Identify an MCP server with its most specific canonical URI: include a scheme, exclude any fragment, prefer the form without a trailing slash unless the slash is semantically significant, and accept uppercase scheme/host on input for robustness.

Make the MCP consent page self-describing and hard to abuse: identify the requesting client by name, show the exact third-party scopes and registered redirect_uri, and protect it with CSRF defenses and anti-clickjacking headers (frame-ancestors CSP or X-Frame-Options: DENY).

Sanitize and validate every URL received from an MCP server: parse strictly, reject shell-special characters, prefer a dedicated sanitization library, and log suspicious authorization URLs for monitoring.

Return the correct HTTP status for authorization errors: 401 when authorization is required or the token is invalid, 403 for invalid scopes or insufficient permissions, and 400 for a malformed authorization request.
Enforce communication security: serve all authorization-server endpoints over HTTPS, restrict every redirect URI to localhost or HTTPS, and follow OAuth 2.1 Section 1.5.

Protect against open redirection: pre-register redirect URIs, have the authorization server validate them by exact match, avoid redirecting user agents to untrusted URIs (auto-redirecting only trusted ones), and have clients use and verify the state parameter, discarding mismatched or missing state.

Treat every server-supplied OAuth discovery URL as untrusted and apply SSRF defenses: require HTTPS in production, block private/reserved and cloud-metadata IP ranges, use a vetted library instead of hand-rolled IP validation, apply the same checks to redirect targets, prefer an egress proxy for server-side deployments, and pin DNS between check and use.

Use short-lived credentials and mutual TLS for endpoint authentication and apply zero-trust continuous verification, re-authenticating and re-authorizing every request rather than granting persistent privileges.

Clients MUST implement PKCE (S256 when technically capable) and verify PKCE support before authorizing by checking code_challenge_methods_supported in the authorization-server (or OpenID provider) metadata, refusing to proceed when it is absent; OpenID-Connect-Discovery authorization servers MUST publish this field.
Require PKCE in MCP OAuth client flows to strengthen the baseline against common OAuth attack classes.

Never accept mis-audienced tokens or pass a client-supplied token through to downstream services: audience-validation failure lets attackers reuse tokens across services and token passthrough creates confused-deputy exposure.

Secure any cookie used to record consent: use the __Host- prefix with Secure, HttpOnly and SameSite=Lax, sign it or back it with a server-side session, and bind it to the specific client_id rather than a generic 'user consented' flag.

Run a strict OAuth state lifecycle: generate a cryptographically random state per request, persist it server-side only after the user approves consent and set the tracking cookie immediately before the third-party redirect, then at the callback require an exact state match, reject missing/mismatched state, and make state single-use with a short expiry.
Validate redirect_uri by exact string match against the registered value and reject any request whose redirect_uri changed without re-registration; never use wildcard or pattern matching.

When sessions are used for state, make session IDs secure random values (e.g., UUIDs from a CSPRNG), bind them to user-specific identity such as <user_id>:<session_id>, and rotate or expire them to limit hijacking impact.

Allowlist authorization-URL schemes: permit only http/https (https in production), reject javascript:, data:, file:, vbscript: and other dangerous schemes, and prefer allowlist over blocklist validation to prevent XSS via malicious authorization URLs.

Open authorization URLs without a shell: never invoke cmd.exe/sh/PowerShell to open URLs, use platform non-shell openers, and web clients should apply a restrictive CSP (script-src/default-src 'self') to block injected JavaScript and command injection.

Close the stdio proxy escalation path by eliminating its enabling vulnerabilities (OAuth URL validation, CSP, input sanitization) and hardening the proxy itself: sandbox/containerize spawned processes, restrict their filesystem access, log stdio usage, require extra authorization for dangerous commands, and isolate proxy communication with least privilege.

Before securing an MCP system, classify its deployment pattern (all-local, single-tenant hybrid, or multi-tenant cloud) and explicitly map the resulting trust boundaries, because security posture is set by where server code originates, where it executes, and what resources it can reach.

Govern the full MCP server lifecycle: mandatory code-signing and binary authorization before install, private vetted repositories with software-composition analysis, allow-lists with documented reviews, SBOM tracking, hash-pinned dependencies and reproducible builds, a centralized server inventory, automated shadow-deployment discovery, deprecation and rollback policies, periodic re-certification, and forced upgrades for servers with known vulnerabilities.

Harden according to the deployment pattern: for all-local use stdio transport (which eliminates DNS-rebinding risk) plus sandboxing; for single-tenant remote require client-server authentication, secure OS-keychain/secret-manager credential storage, and authenticated encrypted channels with enforced server allowlists; for multi-tenant require strong tenant isolation (per-tenant encryption, RBAC), preference for provider-hosted servers over third-party, and remote attestation where possible.

Continuously detect and eliminate shadow, zombie, and malicious MCP servers through automated discovery, a centralized inventory, and decommissioning, because absent provenance and inventory controls attackers deploy unauthorized servers and distribute malicious or rug-pull packages that introduce unvetted capabilities.

Apply segregation-of-access and zero-trust principles because concentrating access to disparate services in one MCP protocol layer violates segregation and its optimistic client/server trust model lets a single compromise cascade into a full breach.

Establish explicit trust boundaries/zones between MCP components, gate dynamic tool discovery behind origin verification or authorization, align tools and models to data-classification zones, prefer local MCP servers for private data, and control egress via a filtering proxy or DLP.

Treat MCP's security as implementation-dependent rather than protocol-guaranteed: adopt it with caution and heightened scrutiny—drawing on lessons from prior distributed and plugin ecosystems—especially in national-security or other high-assurance environments.

Bound every MCP agent with unique identity, documented least-privilege scopes, policy-as-code enforcement, just-in-time elevation for risky access, continuous entitlement review, runtime guardrails, tamper-evident action logs, and separation of permission-granting from deployment authority.

Prevent shadow MCP deployments by requiring central registration before deployment, CI/CD gates, owner and compliance metadata, continuous discovery, secure baseline templates, central IAM, service identities, segmentation, anomaly monitoring, developer education, policy signoff, threat-hunting playbooks, and incident workflows.

Treat MCP context as a boundary-sensitive asset and enforce strict context isolation and lifecycle controls with per-user, per-agent, per-workflow, and per-tenant namespaces, isolated retrieval stores, sensitivity tagging, TTL and purge, pre-storage redaction, approval and preview for sensitive sharing, access logging, injection filtering, and contamination remediation.
Separate sensitive MCP servers from general-purpose servers so payment, authentication, and personal-data capabilities are not exposed to broad shared contexts.
Treat each connected MCP server as a separate untrusted security domain and monitor or mediate cross-server data flows.
Model MCP integrations around explicit host, client, server, data-source, and remote-service responsibilities so capability ownership and access boundaries stay clear.
Treat MCP as a privileged enterprise integration layer and explicitly model trust boundaries for authentication, token movement, tool metadata, runtime execution, and supply-chain provenance.
Map MCP server identities to their required permissions and remediate overprivileged servers before lower-impact posture findings.

Secure MCP source, dependency, build, and release pipelines with controlled environments, reproducible builds, dependency records, signatures, checksums, attestations, version pinning, and strict dependency management.

Treat MCP auto-installers as privileged supply-chain components that must show provenance, verify trusted signatures or checksums, reject mismatches, require confirmation, and isolate setup execution.

Cloud-hosted MCP deployments must pair scaling convenience with managed authentication, scoped authorization, secure session state, privacy controls, data residency handling, latency design, tenant isolation, and runtime sandboxing.

Benchmark MCP defenses across multiple attack types, hosts, and client configurations, then prefer layered defenses combining identity, policy, scanning, detection, arbitration, logging, firewalling, gateways, and isolation.

Contain blast radius with least-privilege scoping per server, because each MCP server has autonomy over tool exposure and scope, so one compromised endpoint can cascade through dependent agents into systemic risk.

Structure robust MCP security as five defense-in-depth layers with no single layer sufficient: provenance verification for authenticity, access control for authorization, context validation for semantic inputs, isolation and protocol integrity to contain operational risk, and continuous monitoring for adaptive feedback.

Harden default MCP deployments with read-only modes, mandatory authentication, and a request/response-validating proxy, and prefer secure-by-design server templates with built-in OAuth, logging, and safe parsing that strips dangerous content from tool descriptions.

Classify an MCP server's authorization into one of three patterns — (1) no checks with implicit trust, (2) authorize-once-and-cache bound to the server or resource but not the caller, or (3) caller-bound with re-authorization on a new caller — and treat only pattern 3 as providing meaningful isolation between invocation contexts.

Prioritize review of developer-facing MCP servers: they dominate the ecosystem, expose dense execution interfaces (over 50% insecure), and often aggregate multiple powerful capabilities, so a single authorization failure can escalate into diverse, high-impact outcomes.

Apply stricter privacy and access controls to MCP server categories that handle sensitive data - external data tools, web-browser content, productivity and collaboration, cloud storage, and communication - since they can expose PII, credentials, or message data.

Threat-model MCP differently from conventional multi-component systems: an LLM whose behaviour is driven by natural-language input sits at the centre of security-critical decisions, and developers must not assume the model will invoke tools safely.

Account for MCP's inherent architectural weaknesses when threat modeling: centralized credential stores are high-value targets, the spec lacks native fine-grained authorization, LLMs transform but do not sanitize malicious input, and there is no control-plane/data-plane separation so any adversary-controllable input can alter execution flow.
Threat-model MCP line jumping for downstream effects such as code exfiltration, vulnerability insertion, and security-alert manipulation, even when the malicious server is never explicitly invoked.
Use lifecycle-centric MCP threat modeling that covers creation, deployment, operation, maintenance, attacker type, threat origin, consequence, supply-chain risk, and LLM-specific tool risks.

Evaluate MCP security as an LLM-tool safety problem that includes prompt manipulation, unsafe execution, untrusted endpoints, unsafe workflows, ambiguous documentation, model behavior, and alignment tradeoffs.

Treat every MCP integration as a privilege-execution boundary, not a passive text interface: MCP turns the LLM into an active system component with shell-level privileges acting on untrusted context, and the attack surface grows with each connected file, database, or API.

Model each MCP primitive's trust domain separately (Resources = read-only context, Tools = external actions, Prompts = reusable templates), because the single safety perimeter dissolves and a failure in one primitive can escalate into a harmful action executed by another.

Never assume the model reliably separates data from instructions: because MCP blends natural-language prompts with code execution there is no rigorous guarantee an agent will not misinterpret malicious input, so a high-privilege LLM can be tricked into running unintended SQL or shell commands (confused deputy).

Do not secure MCP as merely an API or merely an LLM: coupling Context (Resources) with Action (Tools) creates a semantic attack surface where indirect prompt injection escalates into real-world operational damage and epistemic failures such as hallucinations become security breaches, so existing defenses are necessary but insufficient.

Require identity that is traceable end-to-end across the execution chain (initiating user or agent, intermediate MCP servers, and the tools that act), preferring emerging cryptographic workload-identity standards such as SPIFFE/SPIRE where available.

Enforce least-privilege secure delegation for MCP servers using OAuth: authenticate users via existing OIDC identity providers, register servers as IAM clients (using Dynamic Client Registration when needed), never pass through user-provided tokens, perform token exchange for accountability, minimize scopes, and use short-lived proof-of-possession tokens and Rich Authorization Requests; this also defeats confused-deputy abuse.

Verify MCP server provenance before deployment: require developers to publish code signatures and SBOMs, verify contents and signatures against an approved-source and signing-key policy, protect all data in transit with TLS, and prefer end-to-end signatures proving authenticity of returned resources.

Sign and verify MCP messages at the payload level with cryptographic signatures, expiration timestamps, and replay-protection metadata; never assume transport-layer encryption provides message integrity or authenticity.

Handle MCP credentials as ephemeral, scoped, vault-backed secrets: inject them only at runtime, keep them out of model context and stored diagnostics, redact sensitive records, audit credential flows, and rotate immediately on suspected exposure.

Treat MCP schemas, tool manifests, descriptors, and signed tool definitions as executable contracts: require author identity and signature or hash verification, immutable governed version control, semantic policy checks, provenance logging, schema pinning, revalidation before use, approval for high-impact behavior, and rollback plus forensic response after compromise.

Secure the MCP software supply chain by requiring signed provenance for components, deployment SBOM and cryptographic inventories, pinned approved sources, dependency and code scanning, and sandboxed third-party plugins with constrained network and filesystem access.

Use agent passports, trust levels, capability lists, mutual authentication, revocation, and self-hostable trust authority operations to bind MCP agent identity, permissions, and server acceptance to verifiable credentials.
Plan MCP client identity for open-web scale; avoid designs that require every client developer to pre-register with every MCP server operator.
Prefer Client ID Metadata Documents for scalable MCP client identity: clients identify with controlled metadata URLs and authorization servers fetch metadata from those URLs.

Prevent server impersonation by binding MCP namespaces to verified publishers, enforcing uniqueness, surfacing provenance, preferring trusted servers, and monitoring suspicious registration or update behavior.
Resolve MCP tools by verified server-qualified identity and show provenance or trust level before sensitive automatic invocations, with load-time conflict checks across connected servers.
For MCP in smart, industrial, or enterprise automation environments, require secure firmware updates, strict device authentication, and MCP-aware intrusion detection.

Require identity-bound server authentication and integrity or signature verification, because without them tool shadowing, model-switching, unauthorized context injection, and unverified message modification grant attackers silent control.

Deploy MCP zero-trust: identity-bound authentication across Host, Client, and Server; tightly scoped OAuth authorization; signed packages and tool definitions; and provenance/audit trails verifiable before execution.

Honor data-minimization and purpose-limitation (GDPR-style) for MCP workflows that shuttle personal data: label personal data, ensure user consent, keep access audit logs, and enforce strict context isolation with encryption in transit and at rest plus per-layer access controls to prevent cross-tenant leakage.

As a mid-term step, move from implicit trust to explicit verification: enforce tool signatures and immutable versioning via ETDI, and deploy identity-aware proxies that bind every MCP request to a specific user identity so an agent cannot escalate privileges beyond the invoking user, solving the confused-deputy problem.

Treat MCP authorization weakness as systemic — spanning functional categories, star ranges, and maturity, and stemming from flawed assumptions about execution context and caller identity rather than absent checks — and do not assess ecosystem or server security by counting vulnerable servers alone; weigh the nature and severity of the actions those servers enable.

Flag MCP servers that authenticate once at initialization with high-privilege credentials (for example Slack tokens or AWS SDK credentials) and reuse that state for all invocations: they become long-lived, high-privilege API proxies, letting any entity that can invoke the tools perform privileged third-party operations without holding credentials, and because the operations use valid credentials, external services cannot distinguish abuse from intended behavior — enabling stealthy cross-system privilege abuse with limited forensic visibility.
Mitigate MCP server sensitive-API risk with regular dependency checks, sandboxed execution of network and file operations, and standardized authentication for sensitive calls.

Enforce robust access-control models (RBAC or ABAC) at every endpoint, evaluating identity-provider claims such as role, job title, or location, optionally using policy engines like OPA, Cedar, or OpenFGA.

Enforce strong MCP authentication and authorization with mutual authentication, short-lived scoped and bound tokens, server-side validation, per-request deny-by-default RBAC or ABAC, lifecycle controls, least privilege, centralized IAM and policy decisions, secure endpoint defaults, and immediate credential incident response.

Treat all tool descriptions, annotations, schemas, and retrieved resource content as untrusted unless obtained from a trusted server, because tool poisoning, full-schema poisoning, resource-content poisoning, typosquatting, and shadow servers can inject malicious behaviour or instructions.

Strictly validate and sanitize every input with allowlists at each trust boundary (path canonicalization, parameterized queries, context-aware output encoding for SQL/shell/HTML), treat AI-generated content as untrusted requiring the same validation, and deploy prompt-injection detection with strict schemas across all MCP-returned data.
Treat tool metadata and tool outputs as untrusted prompt-injection surfaces, and inspect, sanitize, or constrain them before they influence model behavior.
Treat user, retrieval, API, email, website, and document content as untrusted data that must be sanitized, bounded, and separated from instructions before agent use.
Use an isolated validation or summarization step for untrusted source content when downstream reasoning needs that content but should not directly consume raw instructions from it.
Audit logs and tool-call displays should reveal actual destinations, arguments, and data movements so malicious behavior cannot hide behind ordinary trusted-tool usage.
Normalize and evaluate suspicious structured-context payloads in tool outputs, because injections may imitate surrounding serialization rather than appear as plain instructions.

Validate tool definitions before model-context injection, hash reviewed tool descriptions at deployment, verify each tools/list response against those hashes, and reject changed descriptions as unreviewed model-trusted behavior.

Treat all contextual and Resource input (documents, pasted text, retrieved content, emails, Slack) as untrusted rather than authoritative, because obfuscated embedded directives can redirect tool calls (indirect prompt injection).

Standardize and enforce a tool-metadata schema that structurally separates instructions from descriptive text, because inconsistent implementations (auth varying from unencrypted HTTP to OAuth, varying tool-description formats) create a weakest-link problem.

Assume prompt injection is possible whenever untrusted input can reach the LLM's context window, and never rely on model-level safety controls (trained refusals, classifiers) as an ironclad security boundary.
Treat every MCP sampling prompt supplied by a server as untrusted input that crosses a security boundary before reaching the LLM.

Use one unified threat model in which security breaches and safety failures converge: an indirect prompt injection can cause an honestly-mistaken destructive action, and a tool-parameter hallucination can cause a breach, so never triage epistemic errors and unauthorized actions as separate domains.

Defend the long-context safety blind spot where a prompt injection is buried deep in a long context to evade filters tuned on shorter prompts: train on long-context safety data, scan context in sliding-window segments with safety classifiers, add hierarchical oversight that detects contradictions of earlier policy, and dynamically mask or tag malicious context so the decoder gives it no weight.

Counter prompt injection with layered, patchable defenses (input filters, context compartmentalization, least privilege, output checks), because it is the top-ranked OWASP LLM risk and has no single silver bullet.
Minimize user-facing consent and permission prompts and design them to avoid approval fatigue, since excessive prompts cause habituation and blind approval of dangerous actions.
Protect the integrity and confidentiality of tools and resources with cryptographic checks such as message authentication codes, digital signatures, and encryption.

Use hardware TEEs with remote attestation to isolate MCP clients and servers from compromised hardware, malicious infrastructure operators, and co-tenancy threats, rejecting shadow or compromised servers whose measurements fail attestation, but always complement TEEs with runtime controls because they do not cover vulnerabilities in the running code.

Secure MCP deployments with defense-in-depth—zero-trust architecture, hardware isolation via TEEs, rigorous supply-chain vetting, and continuous monitoring—because documented incidents show that failures of authentication, session management, and supply-chain control are active, not theoretical, threats.

Validate and pin tool metadata and surface complete tool definitions to the approver before execution, because context/tool poisoning hides malicious instructions in tool metadata, schema, or docstrings that agents follow blindly.

Provide a unified tool registry with a schema-validation endpoint that distinguishes benign from malicious tool definitions, because mutable, ambiguous tool definitions enable poisoning, puppet, and rug-pull attacks and standard MCP implementations lack this.

Expose the agent's true context view to the user and use transparency dashboards (such as ScanMCP) that compare what the agent sees versus what the user sees and audit all tool metadata, because a poisoned tool description can drive a hidden malicious action while the agent reports a benign one.

Treat liability for MCP-agent harm as shared and act accordingly: deploying organizations must exercise due care by configuring permissions properly and testing the system, vendors may need to warrant safety features, and an AI governance committee should oversee it.

Recognize that MCP tools often run with the AI system's permissions, so a malicious tool or compromised open-source dependency can be far more damaging than a typical dependency (reading private conversations, accessing internal databases, or impersonating the user), and scope them accordingly.

Treat every tool's metadata — its name and natural-language description loaded at MCP registration — as untrusted data, never as instructions the agent may obey; a description must not be able to add steps to a tool's operation or invoke other tools.

Defend Tool Poisoning at the pre-execution reasoning stage: screen tool descriptions before they enter the agent's planning context rather than relying on content-based output filtering or model safety alignment, which do not catch TPA (refusal stays under 3%).

Identify the security-relevant tool entry as the moment a protocol-level tools/call invocation commits to concrete execution — not an exported function or callback — because MCP dispatch is dynamic and implementation-specific (name-to-handler maps, generic dispatchers, layered callbacks, runtime-built handlers, decorators, add-tool APIs, FastAPI-MCP routes, ToolHandler subclasses); cover all dispatch and registration mechanisms rather than a single syntactic pattern.
Block or require explicit escalation for tool-description instructions that request sensitive-file access, credential handling, covert exfiltration, or concealment from the user.
Treat attacker-controlled content as executable-looking instruction data and do not rely on the model to infer that it has lower authority than user or system instructions.

Block or escalate any flow where a low-trust Resource triggers a destructive Tool on a high-privilege Server, because cross-primitive execution is the most severe indirect-prompt-injection risk, escalating epistemic harm into operational harm.
Prevent cross-primitive indirect-prompt-injection escalation with capability-based Tool permissions, robust semantic filtering, and sanitization of Resource inputs.

Use capability-based access control that couples privileges to specific actions rather than user identity: issue tools fine-grained, scope-bound tokens (read-only, network-isolated) that cannot be reused outside their scope so a compromised tool cannot escalate privileges.
Preserve explicit user intent over tool-description instructions; if metadata conflicts with the requested recipient, destination, or action, stop and surface the conflict.
Before executing external-send tools, inspect and constrain outgoing arguments for unexpected destinations, hidden payloads, and inclusion of prior chat, contact, or history data.
Treat externally received communication content in tool results as adversarial data and prevent it from creating memory, policy, or send-parameter instructions.
Inspect incoming sampling requests for prompt-injection syntax, role or system-message impersonation, and hidden encodings before forwarding them to the LLM.
Design tool-call confirmation screens to expose the complete destination and payload in a reviewable form, with overflow, truncation, and whitespace-based hiding made visible.
Keep the active MCP server set minimal by disabling servers that are not needed for the current workflow.
Isolate host sessions so MCP context from one user, workflow, or client connection cannot bleed into another.
Keep MCP secrets out of static plaintext configuration by using secret managers or encrypted stores, restrictive permissions, token expiration, and automatic rotation.
Model outbound capability broadly: HTTP requests, image loads, API calls, public writes, and generated links can all be exfiltration paths if they can encode private context.
Review aggregate tool composition, not just individual tools, because safe-looking components can become unsafe when their combined capabilities satisfy the lethal trifecta.
Classify email and similar message-reading tools as untrusted-input channels and isolate them from permissions that can expose private data or perform outbound actions.
Frame prompt-injection reviews around trusted and untrusted content sharing model context with tool actions, rather than treating the issue as ordinary jailbreak or model-embarrassment behavior.
Preserve client-side mediation for server-initiated LLM use, including explicit controls over model access, privacy exposure, and cost.
Detect resource-abuse attempts by comparing sampled-token volume and sampling frequency against operation-specific baselines and caps.
Make sampled outputs auditable enough that hidden generated content cannot be concealed by UI summarization or result condensation alone.
Prevent sampled response text from becoming durable behavioral instruction for later turns unless it has passed an explicit trust and safety check.
Constrain sampling-triggered tool access by server capability declarations and by separating one server's authority from tools exposed by other servers.
Scope security conclusions about MCP sampling attacks to the host implementation and surface any assumptions about output handling or permission prompts.

Confine each tool execution to an isolated, short-lived context using sandboxing such as a capability-based microkernel (seL4) or a syscall-intercepting user-space kernel (gVisor) to minimize the host kernel attack surface.
Build sampling prompts from strict templates that isolate trusted task scaffolding from server-supplied and user-supplied content.
Filter sampled completions for unexpected tool calls, future-turn directives, client-behavior changes, malicious destinations, and exploit references.
Keep server-initiated sampling context-minimal so unrelated conversation history is not exposed to or influenced by the requesting server.
Define and test fail-closed behavior for MCP server unavailability before production use.
Govern MCP server supply chains with an approved-server allowlist, cryptographic signing, attestation, version pinning, and runtime checks for behavior changes after installation.

Treat insecure MCP authorization as the common case, not the exception — measured at 46.4% of 6,137 real-world servers, persisting across all functional domains — so assume an unaudited MCP server is likely insecure until verified.
For action-capable MCP assistants and IDE integrations, evaluate data compatibility, permission management, isolation, distributed-call latency, and tool chaining risk.

For static dependency and authorization analysis of MCP server code, AST-level analysis (for example CodeQL) balances precision and recall; improve dependency-reconstruction precision with context-sensitive function-versus-variable distinction, type-based filtering of container abstractions (List/Dict/Optional), explicit callback-parameter tracing for lambdas and higher-order functions, and loop-aware dependency tracking.
Counter vulnerable-version redeployment with automated vulnerability detection, version freshness checks, standardized packaging, and a trusted MCP registry.

Verify a tool's code or definition against a known-good signature or hash as OS package managers do and warn on unexpected change; until such integrity mechanisms exist, pin tool versions and manually inspect updates, because a benign tool can silently auto-update or be modified server-side to reroute API keys.

Concentrate interception and approval at the Host as the policy enforcement point and security boundary (the LLM never touches a data source directly), and do not let Human-in-the-Loop approval be the only line of defense.

Isolate tool namespaces and reject naming collisions, because namespace collisions and command overlap in registries without isolation permit confused-deputy access and escalate in multi-tenant deployments.

Impose call, iteration, retrieval, and CPU/memory quotas, because MCP denial-of-service is unbounded consumption (excessive tool calls, unbounded retrieval, infinite loops) rather than classical network flooding.

Adopt signing, publisher verification, and reputation mechanisms for MCP registries, because open ecosystems (browser extensions, npm, PyPI) moved to these controls after supply-chain abuse and MCP faces the same tool-name collisions, malicious servers, and weak integrity checks.

Account for concentration and propagation of insecurity in the MCP ecosystem: a few marketplaces aggregate roughly two-thirds of servers and act as propagation points, and vulnerable servers cluster among a few prolific authors (the top authors by server count are also the top by vulnerable-server count, with about a third of their servers vulnerable), so reuse amplifies a single source's flaws across many servers.

Measure a decentralized MCP ecosystem with per-registry adapters plus schema inference and canonicalization into a unified schema, because registries differ in data model and access method (HTML pages, JSON APIs, static catalogs).

Guard the retrieval-to-action path and prefer high-fidelity retrieval, because epistemic errors or malicious upstream retrieval propagate downstream into operational harm, and a low-fidelity remote retrieval strategy fragments context and makes epistemic errors likely.

Keep policy and guardrails consistent from Host to Server and do not delegate safety decisions to independently-governed Servers, because scaling alignment requires consistent reward modeling across the environment and delegation lets a remote component circumvent the Host's guardrails.
Propagate safety policies consistently across Host and Server components using a distributed policy-orchestration approach rather than per-component policies.

Strengthen oversight with distributed tracing and forensics rather than relying on log volume, because remote JSON-RPC reasoning intensifies the black-box effect, agents can strategically filter Resource retrievals (deceptive alignment) and misgeneralize goals, and log volume causes reviewer alert fatigue.

Assess aggregate and scale misuse, not only per-call risk: at scale MCP systems exposing sensitive Resources form de facto surveillance architectures, and Tools that send messages or modify files can be weaponized for disinformation or internal compromise.

Treat an MCP system that can modify databases or send emails as potentially high-risk under the EU AI Act and NIST AI RMF, requiring stringent risk management, documentation, human oversight, logging of all tool invocations, regular connector security audits, and incident-response plans.

Note this is the first large-scale empirical measurement of MCP scale and security, and that independent prior work (Li et al.) corroborates that network and system APIs dominate servers and that low-download plugins embed high-risk calls.
Require provenance metadata for every Resource retrieval, including source authority, chunking methodology, and timestamps.

Adopt signed tool manifests with immutable version identifiers and registry-based approval (ETDI): sign each manifest's schema, permissions, and metadata with the provider's key and verify the signature at both load and invocation time, requiring a new signature and explicit re-authorization for any functional change.

Maintain a canonical (centralized or federated) registry as the record of truth for public keys, signed definitions, and change logs, and have hosts cross-check local tool metadata against registry entries and reject mismatches.

Bind every message to a verified, versioned schema record with signed headers backed by a canonical registry record, changelog, and transparency log, so any tool invocation can be verified against an auditable record.

Separate user input, system prompts, and tool-retrieved context with strict delimiters (XML tags or dedicated JSON fields) and instruct the model to treat only content outside those separators as system commands.
Apply deterministic filters, output encoding, and content sanitization to all external tool outputs so external data cannot be parsed as an instruction or code payload.

Isolate executable instructions from content and filter user-provided data for injection patterns (such as 'ignore previous' or 'system:') before it reaches an agent that holds powerful rights, sanitizing tool descriptions so they cannot carry executable instructions.

Run continuous monitoring as a closed loop across Policy/Governance/Compliance, Runtime-Execution, and Detection/Analytics planes, materializing risk directives into concrete tool scopes, execution filters, and isolation rules that define an operational envelope preserving control-flow integrity.

Emit granular telemetry of the agent's internal decisions and tool paths so any outcome can be traced back to its originating prompt and plan, establishing provenance and mitigating accountability obfuscation.

Weigh the interoperability-versus-cost tradeoff of a registry-based zero-trust approach, which improves interoperability by trusting only signed, registered tools but adds latency and reduces flexibility.

Apply a tiered trust model that balances open innovation against security: Tier 0 untrusted tools run in ephemeral, network-gated sandboxes (WebAssembly or gVisor) with no persistent host file-system access; Tier 1 verified, signed tools run with standard permissions but require human-in-the-loop confirmation for high-risk actions; Tier 2 hardened, formally verified core tools run with high autonomy under continuous runtime audit and anomaly detection.

To apply a uniform allow/deny or safety policy across MCP and competing standards such as OpenAI function calling or Microsoft plugins, establish shared schemas, common tool-definition ontologies, and policy-interchange formats.

Surface safety controls in the user experience (for example toggles or sliders for permitted action classes) rather than hiding them in config files, and keep them minimally intrusive by explaining why an action was blocked, because acceptable risk varies by environment and over-inconvenient controls drive users to workarounds.

Never let an assistant ingest untrusted content channels while holding powerful credentials: in the 2025 Supabase incident an instruction hidden in a support ticket was later ingested as context and executed as SQL under service_role credentials, exfiltrating a sensitive tokens table into a customer-visible thread.

Protect the integrity of the RAG corpus and retriever, because inserting only a few malicious documents or backdooring the retriever can achieve high-success-rate prompt injection such as malware links or denial-of-service.

Prevent cross-tenant leakage through shared efficiency optimizations: sharing key-value caches or vector indexes across tenants creates covert side channels even without an explicit bug (the PROMPTPEEK attack reconstructs another user's prompt token by token from cache hits), so relax separation for efficiency only with provable safety or not at all.

Enforce strict per-tenant context isolation as mechanism: disable cache sharing across users, partition vector stores per tenant with namespace filters or separate indexes, tag every request with a tenant identifier, and have every internal component (LLM, retriever, cache) check a per-request tenant access token before serving any data.

Unify siloed policy layers under one coherent, federated governance framework, because policy-conflict failures occur when misaligned model content filters, business rule engines, and data-access controls collide and produce either a security lapse or a functional breakdown, and MCP integrates many such components.

Unify data-confidentiality policies into the AI's own instructions, because a confused-deputy failure arises when a rule such as row-level security is enforced only for human interfaces while the agent holds a credential that ignores it and has no awareness of the rule.

Test AI pipelines for policy adherence by crafting adversarial scenarios that put the AI's policies at odds, including simulating a rogue instruction, to verify that human data policies still hold and no disallowed data is output.

Translate key business policies into the AI layer by augmenting prompts with company-specific rules (for example, do not expose data marked confidential) and using a post-LLM rule engine or policy DSL to catch disallowed outputs.

Designate a single ultimate gatekeeper for each decision and assume the AI can fail, letting a downstream deterministic system such as a data-loss-prevention or email-security filter have the final check rather than disabling it on the assumption the AI already handled it.
Log not just what the AI did but why (which policy triggered a refusal and which checks passed on an allow), so analysts can refine policies and resolve conflicts explicitly.

Assume a tool may turn malicious and monitor tool behavior at runtime as an intrusion-detection layer, flagging out-of-scope actions such as a calculator tool making network calls or a weather tool returning SSH keys.

Assess security impact with a resource-centric view: classify each tool invocation by the type of resource it ultimately affects — system-level execution, persistent data access, network or external communication, or physical/human-interface interaction — rather than by how the tool is invoked or implemented, and treat system-level execution capabilities as particularly severe.

Use the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications as a deployment checklist, implementing a control for each item (for example prompt filters and input validation for prompt injection, and limiting autonomous actions plus confirmation for high-impact operations for excessive agency).

Align MCP development with the NIST AI RMF phases Identify (catalog components and risk points), Measure (pentest and measure attack-success rates), Manage (deploy mitigations), and Govern (establish oversight), emphasizing continuous monitoring and defense-in-depth.

Prepare AI-specific incident-response playbooks (containment for a model compromised via prompt injection, notification and log-purge for an MCP data leak) and share anonymized post-mortems so lessons roll into updated best practices.
Manage a tool-enabled AI agent across its lifecycle rather than fire-and-forget, as with any critical software service.

Consider that governance may become partly automated through meta-governance watchdog agents that monitor other agents and intervene on policy deviation, consistent with a zero-trust posture in which not even the AI is implicitly trusted.

Anticipate sensory injection attacks now, because as MCP expands beyond text to stream multi-modal contexts such as audio, video, screen sharing, or CCTV feeds it will introduce new classes of injection that defenses must be designed to handle.

Flag a tool description that combines a trigger condition, a malicious/unrelated action, and a plausible justification — this three-part structure is the signature of an effective poisoned description; a payload missing the trigger condition is largely inert.

Do not expect Indirect-Prompt-Injection payloads to transfer to Tool Poisoning: injected verbatim into a tool description they drop to near-0% ASR because they lack a trigger condition and lose contextual prominence — a TPA payload must supply its own trigger context.

Assume the malicious action will be performed by a legitimate, already-registered tool while the poisoned tool is never executed; do not gate solely on 'new or unknown tool', because that stealth pattern is chosen specifically to look unsuspicious and to bypass new-tool permission models.

Enumerate and test all three attack paradigms when assessing an agent: explicit-trigger function hijacking (P1), implicit-trigger function hijacking (P2), and implicit-trigger parameter tampering (P3); covering only one leaves the others unmeasured.

Prioritize defenses against parameter tampering: it is empirically the most effective paradigm (average ASR 46.7% vs 36.7% explicit and 26.7% implicit function hijacking), likely because the primary call still matches user intent and only a single parameter is altered — so validate tool-call parameters against user intent, not just which tool is called.

Do not assume a larger or reasoning-enabled model is safer against Tool Poisoning; inverse scaling holds — more capable models are often more vulnerable (enabling Qwen3 reasoning raised ASR by 27.8%; o1-mini reached 72.8%) because the attack exploits stronger instruction-following.

Do not rely on the agent to defend itself: refusal is negligible (under 3% even for the best-refusing model) and 18.9% of failed attacks are still 'direct execution' of the malicious tool — assume no self-defense and add an external control.

When measuring TPA, define Attack Success narrowly — the agent calls a separate legitimate tool to complete the malicious action — compute ASR over valid outputs only, and record the four-way outcome taxonomy (Success / Ignored / Direct-Execution / Refused) so direct-execution and refusal are not hidden inside a single failure bucket.

Do not treat the presence or absence of classic jailbreak wrappers ('<IMPORTANT>...', 'Ignore all previous instructions...') as a safety signal for TPA: they add only ~2% ASR to a well-formed payload, so a clean-looking description can be fully effective.

Bound Tool-Poisoning risk conclusions to the single-turn setting they were measured in; multi-turn or stateful memory poisoning and sleeper-trigger attacks are unmeasured here and plausibly worse, so do not read these results as an upper bound.
Do not assume the LLM or agent reliably preserves, binds, or forwards user identity; LLMs are often stateless third-party services, so the MCP server itself must establish and verify caller identity.

Treat caller identity confusion as an implementation flaw, not a specification flaw: MCP permits authorization reuse but does not mandate how that state is scoped or attributed, and a server's security is determined by how its tools are implemented, dispatched, and protected — so the fix lies in server implementation.

Assess authorization by attribution: for each tool invocation that reaches a sensitive resource, verify the authorization decision is explicitly scoped to the caller that initiated the invocation — not merely that authorization logic exists somewhere in the code. This is the core stance for detecting caller identity confusion.

Do not infer authorization correctness from the presence of authorization logic, specific APIs, or framework constructs; authorization state may be cached in memory, held as a global flag, tied to a session, or embedded in initialization logic and then reused, and checks are scattered rather than at fixed APIs — so reason about the concrete execution path instead.

Trace the control flow from each tool entry point to every operation that interacts with system, file, network, or physical resources — including sensitive operations reached transitively through helpers or libraries — and along each path determine whether authorization is absent, cached as server-level state, or explicitly bound to the caller identity.

Treat each tool invocation as a distinct security principal whose actions must be individually attributable; do not assume that authorization established earlier in the server lifecycle justifies subsequent executions.

Evaluate authorization along three dimensions: its form (OAuth, bearer token, API key, username/password, or local cached credential), its timing (once at startup versus per tool invocation), and its binding to the caller (dependence on tool input parameters, session identifiers, or execution-context objects).

Recognize the three unsafe-tool classes when auditing: AuthNone (no checks before or during execution), AuthCache (authorization performed once, e.g. at initialization, then cached and reused without re-validation), and AuthRuntime (runtime checks that rely on in-memory state or are applied inconsistently across invocations); AuthCache in particular persists in long-lived, infrastructure-oriented tools.

Combine developer-enforced session and caller-identity management (which aligns with MCP's execution model and gives fine-grained control over authorization scope) with static detection tools that identify where caller-identity or session binding is missing or inconsistently enforced in existing implementations.

Do not use GitHub stars or popularity as evidence of authorization quality; insecure patterns (including no-authorization and inconsistent runtime-authorization) persist even among highly starred projects.

Treat static-analysis detector output as a high-recall screen, not ground truth: reported recall is high (tool extraction ~94-100%, authorization detection ~90-92%, capability detection >94%) but false positives arise mainly from developer-defined helper or wrapper functions that resemble tool entry points, and analysis cost grows with project size (more sharply beyond ~3,000 lines of code) — so confirm flagged entries and budget for larger projects.

Do not treat a fixed command prefix (for example prefixing a shell invocation with git) as a safe constraint: command extensibility such as git config core.editor lets an attacker execute arbitrary shell commands.
Do not rely on OAuth alone to isolate callers: it authenticates users and issues access tokens but does not establish MCP session boundaries or bind authorization to the caller.

Treat raw MCP marketplace project counts as inflated: more than half of listed projects are invalid or low-value, so apply per-market validity rates (roughly 26-43% valid) before citing ecosystem size.

Aggregate across MCP markets for coverage: no single market is complete - only about 32% of projects appear in more than one market and about 5.5% in four or more, while MCP.so holds roughly 89% share but is saturated.

Interpret MCP ecosystem growth cautiously: measured scale is smaller than raw counts suggest, MCP.so has plateaued, and new growth is driven largely by duplication (via MCP Market) rather than novel projects.

Choose a marketplace's local vs hosted mode by the control/convenience trade-off: local mode keeps full credential and runtime control in the user's environment, hosted mode gives managed runtime and stable endpoints but delegates execution control to the provider.
For hosts serving heterogeneous queries, consider an optional context resolver that routes each request to the most relevant server by domain, avoiding hardcoded server selection.

Resolve cross-market MCP entities with multi-feature matching (GitHub URL as strong id, TF-IDF cosine text similarity, author and license, temporal activity) plus content hashing; auto-merge above a threshold and escalate borderline cases to human review - never rely on a single identifier.

Exclude low-value MCP entries with rule-based filters: drop placeholder repos (init-only commit or empty README), inactive forks (no independent commits), abandoned projects (last commit over 12 months), and boilerplate templates; flag low-content entries (fewer than 5 source files or missing docs) for review.

Crawl reproducibly and resiliently: rate-limited, robots-aware requests, time-versioned snapshots, rotating IPs, keyword variants, and semi-automated CAPTCHA handling with cookie or session reuse - these lifted coverage about 18% and sustained roughly 36-hour sessions at about 96.7% success.

Rank MCP projects by combining complementary signals - GitHub stars and forks (visibility), security and license ratings, and usage statistics - into a normalized weighted composite score rather than any single source.

Validate automated MCP filtering and scoring against a labeled manual sample and multi-source aggregation: a 500-entry sample gave about 93.5% detection accuracy and composite scoring cut ranking variance about 21% versus single-source.
Prefer JSON or API market sources over HTML scraping where both exist: API crawling has lower parsing overhead and higher throughput.

Expect MCP clients to be more consistently maintained and higher quality than servers (nearly all client entries were valid versus about half of server entries), so apply heavier quality filtering to servers.

Judge an MCP server's security posture from repository signals - project size, lines of code, and commit history - and continuously monitor maintenance: about 21.9% of servers are inactive over a year (an unpatched long tail) and oversized dependency-heavy servers widen the attack surface, while most servers are lightweight.

Treat the MCP ecosystem as transitional - widely adopted in appearance but structurally fragile (over 50% low-value, supply-chain monocultures, uneven maintenance, slow client protocol migration) - and weight advice toward sustainability, server security, and client interoperability.

Require explicit input validation in every MCP server regardless of language: Python and TypeScript get it from pydantic and zod, but Go and Rust serialization libraries (serde, yaml.v3) do not validate, so those servers must implement checks manually to avoid injection or deserialization flaws.

Treat dependency monoculture as systemic risk: Java servers concentrate on Spring (a single flaw like SpringShell can cascade), and over 93% of servers are JavaScript or Python, so a popular npm or PyPI vulnerability can cascade widely - audit and diversify shared dependencies.

Weigh implementation language in server security: memory-safe Rust and stricter-typed Go reduce certain vulnerability classes versus dynamic JavaScript and Python (which add dependency-confusion, prototype-pollution, and insecure-serialization surface), while Java frameworks carry Spring or Log4j-scale exploit risk.

Match client connection mode to use case: single-connection (80.9% of clients) suits vertical, simple deployments with lower session overhead; multi-connection (19.1%) suits integration, enterprise, or IDE scenarios needing aggregation, redundancy, and richer workflows.

Read protocol convergence as a standardization signal: convergence eases integration but reduces diversity, and MCP clients show only gradual, uneven movement toward standardization with persistent legacy (stdio and SSE) reliance and engineering inertia.

Measure ecosystems ethically: use only publicly accessible data, never bypass authentication, crawl private datasets, or degrade server availability, and report aggregate trends rather than detailed exploit paths.
Treat MCP ecosystem findings as a time-bounded snapshot (here a two-week crawl) of a fast-moving ecosystem, not permanent conclusions; re-measure before relying on specific figures.

Remember metadata- and dependency-based measurement understates runtime risk (it misses dynamic loading, undocumented features, and proprietary modules) and that category or protocol classification can misclassify heterogeneous projects - treat such findings as lower bounds.
